questions.prompt: A container application starts children but does not reap them reliably. What does Docker `--init` add?

sources.title: Docker: Run multiple processes in a container
sources.claim: Docker --init inserts a tiny init process as the main process to handle reaping. It neither installs a full init system, creates VMs nor prevents child processes.

questions.explanation: Docker --init inserts a tiny init process as the main process to handle reaping. It neither installs a full init system, creates VMs nor prevents child processes.

choices.text: A complete systemd installation that automatically supervises every service.
A separate virtual machine that runs each child outside the container.
A tiny init process that handles child-process reaping.
A replacement application runtime that prevents any child from starting.

questions.prompt: A Docker container is running but its HEALTHCHECK fails repeatedly beyond the retry threshold. What state does that check establish?

sources.title: Dockerfile reference: HEALTHCHECK
sources.claim: HEALTHCHECK maintains health state independently of process execution. Repeated failures mark unhealthy. The instruction does not itself remove a container, replace its image or declare it healthy merely because PID 1 runs.

questions.explanation: HEALTHCHECK maintains health state independently of process execution. Repeated failures mark unhealthy. The instruction does not itself remove a container, replace its image or declare it healthy merely because PID 1 runs.

choices.text: The container automatically receives a new image and restarts with it.
The container is removed because a failing check is an exit instruction.
The container is healthy if its main process has not exited unexpectedly.
The container health status becomes unhealthy.

questions.prompt: For a public GitHub repository using default fork pull-request settings, which workflow security statements hold? Select all that apply.

sources.title: GitHub Actions: Events that trigger workflows
sources.claim: A describes the default restricted fork context. C explains why pull_request_target needs extra care. B is false because the default fork token is read-only. D and E are false: untrusted contributor code remains untrusted and the event does not sanitize it.

questions.explanation: A describes the default restricted fork context. C explains why pull_request_target needs extra care. B is false because the default fork token is read-only. D and E are false: untrusted contributor code remains untrusted and the event does not sanitize it.

choices.text: Ordinary fork `pull_request` runs do not receive repository secrets.
The default fork pull-request token has write access to repository contents.
`pull_request_target` runs in the trusted base-repository context.
Untrusted head code is safe to execute with secrets because a maintainer opened the workflow.
Switching to `pull_request_target` automatically sanitizes contributor scripts.

questions.prompt: A container starts several subprocesses. Which process-lifecycle responsibility does Docker document for its main process?

sources.title: Docker: Run multiple processes in a container
sources.claim: The main container process is responsible for managing children. An init helper can address deficient reaping. Children are not independent containers, and rebuilding an image is not lifecycle cleanup.

questions.explanation: The main container process is responsible for managing children. An init helper can address deficient reaping. Children are not independent containers, and rebuilding an image is not lifecycle cleanup.

choices.text: Delegate every child to the host shell, which always reaps it immediately.
Leave every terminated child in place until the container image is rebuilt.
Treat each child as an independent container with its own automatic lifecycle.
Manage the processes it starts, including their cleanup.

questions.prompt: During a Docker HEALTHCHECK start period, one check succeeds before later checks fail. What changes after that success?

sources.title: Dockerfile reference: HEALTHCHECK
sources.claim: A success during the start period marks startup complete; later consecutive failures count. The grace period is not restarted per failure, and one success does not disable checking.

questions.explanation: A success during the start period marks startup complete; later consecutive failures count. The grace period is not restarted per failure, and one success does not disable checking.

choices.text: Later failures count toward the unhealthy retry threshold.
Every later failure is ignored until the original start period has elapsed.
The start period begins again after every later failing health check.
The successful check disables health checking until the container restarts.

questions.prompt: A privileged `pull_request_target` workflow labels pull requests. Which boundaries should its author understand? Select all that apply.

sources.title: GitHub Actions: Events that trigger workflows
sources.claim: A: the event uses the base repository. B: privileged execution of untrusted head code risks secrets and other resources. E: labeling is a suitable metadata task. C is false because the event confers no code trust; D ignores its different privileges.

questions.explanation: A: the event uses the base repository. B: privileged execution of untrusted head code risks secrets and other resources. E: labeling is a suitable metadata task. C is false because the event confers no code trust; D ignores its different privileges.

choices.text: Its context is the base repository rather than the fork merge branch.
Checking out and running contributor code can expose privileged resources.
Its event name guarantees that downloaded pull-request scripts are trusted.
It always has the same secret restrictions as default fork `pull_request`.
It can perform metadata tasks without executing untrusted head code.
